 [K-Women Talk] When a Leader's Anger Dominates Diplomacy
 Published 26 Oct.2026 11:00(KST) 
 Share 
 Language 
 Text Size 
 Print 
 Overreaction to Ukraine over North Korean POW issue
Demand for apology and recall of ambassador set back bilateral ties
The stronger the leader, the greater the restraint: National interest comes first
 View original image 
 During the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis, a U.S. reconnaissance aircraft was shot down by a Soviet-made missile, killing its pilot. The military called for a military response. But President Kennedy resisted the temptation to retaliate and chose the path of negotiation. Rather than directly confronting Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev's hardline demands, he opened a path out of the crisis by responding to a conciliatory proposal Khrushchev had made earlier. It was not merely the power of great nations that prevented a crisis from spiraling into nuclear war. It was the political judgment to carefully restrain the anger of the top leader.
 A leader's emotions are never a trivial matter in diplomacy. But a leader's anger must not become the anger of the state. No leader can know everything or assess alone the complex context and repercussions of every issue. That is why diplomacy requires an organization with expertise and experience. The role of diplomatic officials is not to read the leader's mood and devise hardline policies, but sometimes to deliver unwelcome truths and prevent an overreaction.
 Recent diplomatic tensions with Ukraine have made it difficult to shake this thought. Over the disclosure that North Korean prisoners of war had been repatriated to South Korea, our government demanded a public apology, recalled its ambassador, and then decided to withdraw some diplomatic mission personnel. A diplomatic protest has resulted in a serious deterioration in relations between the two countries. If a confidential agreement was breached, it is only right to protest and demand corrective action. But do a mere disagreement over the scope of disclosure and a refusal to apologize constitute such a serious infringement of the national interest as to justify measures this severe?
 What diplomacy must guard against most is a leader taking the front line in a conflict. The moment an issue that can be resolved at the working level becomes tied to the authority of the highest leadership, compromise looks like capitulation and concessions become a defeat for the leader. The other side, too, has its own pride that it cannot afford to surrender. Both sides are left with no way out. That is why diplomacy needs to leave leaders room to take a step back.
 We should also reflect on our society's culture of demanding apologies. An apology is a valuable expression that can help restore a relationship, but at times it is corrupted into a ritual for confirming the other party's submission. When the sentiment of power - "How dare they defy our demand?" - enters the picture, an apology becomes not a means of resolving a problem but a token of obedience. It is a paradox: in trying to protect the nation's dignity, we end up narrowing its options.
 We cannot rule out the possibility that political calculations prioritizing relations with North Korea and Russia played a part in the hardline response. From the perspective of those who value restoring ties with Russia, Ukraine may be an inconvenient diplomatic partner. This incident may have been a case of someone looking for an excuse and finding one. It is all the more dangerous if a leader's displeasure and strategic bias reinforce each other. Of course, we cannot presume to know the government's actual motives.
 The costs are by no means small. Recalling the ambassador and then withdrawing diplomatic mission personnel goes beyond a simple protest and reduces diplomatic capacity itself. If channels for cooperation with Ukraine narrow, our capacity to gather information on and respond to military cooperation between North Korea and Russia could also weaken. To Western countries that have kept their embassies in Kyiv despite the Russian threat, South Korea may appear to be stepping back from international solidarity. Such damage to trust is no small matter for South Korea, which relies on international law and norms.
 A strong leader is not one who always responds forcefully. A strong leader is one who can leave open the possibility that their judgment may be wrong and knows how to restrain their anger. A capable diplomatic organization does not justify a leader's anger; it filters that anger so it does not harm the national interest. The success or failure of diplomacy should be judged not by how fully a leader's anger was acted upon, but by what was protected and what was lost for the people. A leader may own the anger, but the people alone bear its costs.
